blog_summary: Adrian Colyer reflects on the 2015 State of DevOps Survey results, which revealed a 200x gap in lead times between the best and worst performers. He draws a parallel to Michael Kremer's 'O-Ring Theory of Economic Development' (1993), which explains how small drops in quality across a production process can lead to dramatic reductions in output. The theory posits that in systems where tasks are interdependent and quality cannot be substituted for quantity, even minor weaknesses can cause catastrophic failures. Colyer applies this model to DevOps, suggesting that small quality gaps in any stage of a pipeline (e.g., testing, deployment) can disproportionately harm overall performance, velocity, and quality. He highlights how high-performing organizations achieve both speed and quality, debunking the trade-off myth, and emphasizes the compounding benefits of incremental improvements in quality.
